posts.author: Aerosys
posts.body:
Theoretically, there's no 100% security. If you have somebody with bad intentions and high motivation, they will break any RPG Maker game.
I personally like publishing RPG Maker games as browser games, because then, you can just play them without downloading first. In this setup, you, as the game dev, can encrypt your plugins in a way that they only run on your site, and nowhere else! In other words, a plugin will check whether the URL of the browser is yours (in my case, play.aerosys.blog), otherwise it will quit the game.

posts.author: Solar_Flare
posts.body:
ValentinaSama67 said:
In the end we are just putting locks on our bikes but there will always be people with cutters to steal them. The lock only discourages your casual thief from taking, but people with bad intetions and high motivation won't be discouraged
Click to expand...
A better analogy would be that we're putting a lock on the bike, but hiding the key to that lock under the seat. No cutters needed – the key is right there.
That's literally what encryption is doing. The files are encrypted, and the key to unlock that encryption is included in an unencrypted file alongside them.
There's no way around this, however. You need to be able to access those files to play the game. If they're encrypted, you can't play the game without the key. This is true even if (as Aerosys mentioned) you only release it as a web game.
The net result is the same though – it only discourages a "casual thief". Anyone who really wants to can find the key and decrypt the files.
Personally, I don't think it's worth doing. But I know lots of people disagree.

posts.author: Ludovinsky
posts.body:
Going commercial actually does change the risk profile a bit.  When you sell a game, you’re not just releasing files. You’re releasing a product with a license, a price tag, and a paper trail. That makes it much easier to prove ownership and take action if someone tries to resell or repackage your work.  Free projects tend to get targeted more often because there’s no commercial footprint, no storefront record, and usually no legal follow through. It’s not that the dev “deserves it,” it’s just that thieves look for the lowest risk targets from my experience observing this industry.
A commercial release signals that the creator is serious, has documentation, and is more likely to defend their work. That alone discourages most bad actors.  Of course, nothing is 100% safe...even AAA games get cracked, but going commercial, using Steam’s DRM, and having clear branding can make your game a much less attractive target.

I just use the encrypt game files option on the deployment page of RPG Maker.
Also, I kinda think like this, if someone actually was motivated enough to steal my game, it would already need to be somewhat well known. posts.author: Solar_Flare
posts.body:
Darkmoon9 said:
Would anyone actually bother stealing a free game?
Click to expand...
The entire game, maybe not. The pieces of the game (assets, code, etc), sure.
Darkmoon9 said:
I would probably be fine with someone else uploading it elsewhere as long as that means greater visibility.
Click to expand...
I'd be okay with this for a free game if the other person properly credited me. But there are still a lot of things that could be called "theft" even for a free game – either improper/false credit, or reusing assets without permission. (Just because a game is free does not mean that its assets are free to be used in other works.)
Note that I don't consider this to be an argument in favour of encrypting your game. The only way to really stop that sort of person is to catch them in the act.
Sure, encrypting your game makes things harder for those people, but it won't stop anyone determined. On the other hand, it theoretically can make things worse for legitimate players, as loading the images and audio now takes longer due to the need to decrypt them at the same time. (I say theoretically because in most real cases that worsening is unnoticeable.)

The other reason is that I tend to have all kinds of random files among the image files in the game, even if it is unused. For some reason if I try to mark exclude unused files, it always fails to launch. Do anyone know why? As a result, my games are always a bit larger than they should be.

posts.author: Solar_Flare
posts.body:
Darkmoon9 said:
For some reason if I try to mark exclude unused files, it always fails to launch. Do anyone know why? As a result, my games are always a bit larger than they should be.
Click to expand...
Ah, that's probably because you use some plugins that don't support the Exclude Unused Files feature. The engine provides ways to make your plugin compatible with it, but in my experience, a lot of plugin authors don't bother.
In most cases, it's not that hard to edit the plugin to make it compatible. For example, I recently edited HO_AchievementSystem for this purpose – it was just about 3 lines added to the comment section. Awhile ago I made SRD_SummonCore compatible with Exclude Unused Files as well – that was quite a bit harder. It's not generic enough to release, I'd need to improve it first. I may have done the same for other plugins but those are the only two I remember.
I'll always be open to helping people make Exclude Unused Files work in their game, if you want to open a separate thread for that. Though, if it's paid plugins (especially VisuStella/Yanfly) I'm not sure to what extent I can actually help. I can still try however.

posts.author: Solar_Flare
posts.body:
I don't know for sure, but it likely isn't.
Given that making the plugin compatible is usually a case of editing the documentation comment, there is a real possibility that I could do it even for VisuStella plugins, since they obviously can't obfuscate the documentation. That's only if it's using standard note tags though (like
<tag:value>
, not
<tag>value</tag>
). Although, to be clear, this only matters for tags where the value is an image or audio file, or an animation ID.
If it's not using standard note tags, the approach I did with SRD_SummonCore (adding a second plugin that parses different note tags into the same data) would probably require actually owning the plugin, so I don't think I'd be able to help with VisuStella in that case.
